h1: Should You Hire a Social Media Manager or an Agency for Your Restaurant?
metaTitle: Restaurant Social Media Manager vs Agency: How to Choose
metaDescription: Restaurant social media manager vs agency vs DIY: honest pros, cons, and cost ranges, plus a simple way to choose based on your budget, time, and stage.
heroAlt: A restaurant owner meeting with a marketing team at a table

Choose based on your budget, your stage, and the hours you can spare.

intro:
You are good at running a restaurant. You are probably not thrilled about spending your one free hour a day figuring out Instagram. So the question shows up sooner or later: should you hire someone to handle your social media, and if so, a single manager or a whole agency? Or should you just keep doing it yourself?

Here is the honest truth up front. There is no single best answer. The right choice depends on three things: how much you can spend, how much time you actually have, and what stage your restaurant is in. A brand-new taco spot in Hialeah and an established Brickell steakhouse opening a second location need completely different help.

This guide lays out all three real options (a manager, an agency, or doing it yourself) with honest pros, cons, and rough costs for each. We will even walk through, click by click, how to find and test someone before you sign anything. By the end you will know which option fits you right now, even if that option is to keep it in-house a while longer.

sections.h2: First, figure out what you actually need (not who to hire)
sections.html:
Before you compare a manager against an agency, get clear on the job itself. Almost every owner asks 'who should I hire' before asking 'what actually needs to happen every week.' Flip that order and the decision gets easy.

Two quick definitions so we are speaking the same language. A social media manager is a single person who runs your accounts. They can be an employee you put on payroll (in-house) or an independent freelancer you pay by the month or the hour. An agency is a company with a small team that runs your social media as a paid service, usually several specialists instead of one generalist.

Now do this five-minute audit before you talk to anyone:

  1. Write down your one main goal. Filling slow weeknights, building a bigger following, promoting a new location, or getting more reservations. One goal, in one sentence.
  2. List what has to happen every week to hit it: feed posts, Stories, short videos (Reels), replying to comments and direct messages, answering Google and Yelp reviews, and running any ads.
  3. Be honest about the content. Someone has to physically show up and film your food, your room, and your busy nights. Fresh footage is the real work. Ask yourself who is going to shoot it.
  4. Add up the hours. Shooting, editing, writing, posting, and replying for a restaurant is usually 5 to 10 hours a week done well. Write down an honest number.
  5. Set a monthly budget range you are comfortable with, before anyone quotes you. Even a rough 'no more than X' keeps you from overbuying.

Those five answers decide everything that follows. If the honest hours are high and you have none to spare, you are heading toward an agency. If the budget is tiny but you have a reliable person, a freelancer or doing it yourself fits. If you want exact dollar figures for every level of service, we break them all down in our guide to what restaurant social media management costs per month.

sections.h2: Option A: Hiring a social media manager (in-house or freelance)
sections.html:
This is the 'one person' option. You hire an individual to own your accounts, either as a part-time or full-time employee, or as a freelancer working remotely for several clients at once.

What you get

Someone who gets to know your restaurant closely: your regulars, your dishes, your voice. A good manager is flexible and personal. You can text them 'we just plated the special, can you post it' and it happens. For one or two platforms and a steady, professional feed, a solid manager is often all you need.

What it costs

A freelancer usually charges $25 to $75 per hour, and many package restaurant work at $800 to $1,500 a month for content, captions, scheduling, and light community management. An in-house hire is a bigger commitment: a full-time social media manager in the Miami area runs roughly $50,000 to $70,000 a year in salary, plus payroll taxes, benefits, and the tools they need. A part-time employee costs less, but also gives you fewer hours. Ad spend is separate either way.

The catch

It is one human being. When they take a vacation, get sick, or sign one client too many, your feed feels it right away. You are also the boss now. You have to hand them direction, review their work, approve posts, and chase them when a week goes quiet. And one person rarely does everything well. A talented writer may not be a strong videographer, so you might still hire a separate photographer for real shoots.

When it is the right call

Pick a manager when your budget is modest, you enjoy staying involved, and you have someone (them or a staffer) who can reliably shoot content. It is a great fit for a stable neighborhood spot that wants a consistent feed without a big monthly agency bill.

How to find and test a freelancer

  1. Ask other local owners first. A referral from a restaurant whose feed you admire beats any online search. Ask them who shoots their content.
  2. Search Instagram. Find local restaurant feeds you like, then check their bio or tagged accounts. Many freelancers and small studios are credited right there.
  3. Ask for a portfolio and two references. You want to see real restaurant work, not general 'social media' samples, and you want to call two current clients.
  4. Ask the three questions that separate pros from posers: How often do you come shoot in person? Is ad spend included in your fee or billed separately? Can you show me a restaurant feed you built from zero?
  5. Start with a paid one-month trial, not a long contract. Judge them on two things: did they post on time, and does the content actually look like your place? If yes, extend. If not, you are only out one month.

An agency is the 'whole team' option. Instead of one generalist, you get a small group of specialists (someone shooting, someone editing, someone writing, someone watching the ad account) running your social media as a service for a monthly fee.

What you get

Coverage that does not disappear when one person is out, because it never rested on one person. Most restaurant agencies bundle photo and video production, content, community management, and paid ads under one roof, so the pieces actually work together. The biggest difference is ownership: a good agency owns the outcome, not just a task list. You approve a plan and they make it happen.

What it costs

Agencies typically start around $1,500 a month and climb from there. A growth program with a monthly in-person shoot, several platforms, and light ad management usually runs $1,800 to $3,000. Full-service work with frequent shoots, daily posting, and serious paid media is $2,500 to $5,000 and up. As always, ad spend is a separate line, usually $500 to $1,500 a month on top. Our own restaurant social media marketing service sits in that team-based model.

The catch

You pay more than you would for a solo freelancer, and that is real money for a small restaurant. You are also one of several clients, so ask up front who your point of contact is and how fast they reply. And you trade some day-to-day control: you approve a monthly plan instead of touching every post, which some owners love and others miss. A weak agency can also be templated and generic, which is exactly why the red flags later in this guide matter.

When it is the right call

Choose an agency when you need consistent output, in-person photo and video, and ads plus content, and you simply do not have the time to manage a hire. It also fits when you are growing fast, running more than two platforms, opening a second location, or you need reliable bilingual coverage for Miami's large Spanish-speaking audience.

An honest word, since we are one

Button Up is an agency, so take this with that in mind: an agency is not automatically the better choice. If your budget is very tight, or you love being hands-on and have the hours, a good freelancer or doing it yourself will beat a cheap, templated agency every time. The right answer is the one that fits your restaurant, not the one with the biggest team.

sections.h2: Option C: Doing it yourself (or handing it to a staff member)
sections.html:
The third option is the one most restaurants start with: you run it yourself, or you hand it to a server or manager who is 'good with phones.'

What you get

The cheapest and, honestly, sometimes the most authentic content there is. Nobody knows your food and your regulars like you do. You can post a special the second it comes out of the kitchen, with no approval chain and no waiting. Full control, zero monthly invoice.

What it costs

Nothing in dollars, and a lot in time. Doing it well is 5 to 10 hours a week, plus a few small tools: a phone tripod or gimbal, a simple editing app, and maybe a scheduling tool. If a staff member handles it, the cost is their hourly wage for those hours, plus the very real risk that it gets dropped the moment the dining room fills up.

The catch

Consistency, almost every time. Social media is the first thing that falls off the list on a busy Friday, and a feed that goes quiet for three weeks undoes months of work. Quality also tends to plateau, and nobody on your staff is likely an expert at paid ads. Burnout is real. Plenty of owners try in-house first, then move to a freelancer or agency once they see how uneven it gets.

A do-it-yourself routine that actually holds up

  1. Pick one platform. For most restaurants that is Instagram. Do one thing well before adding TikTok or anything else.
  2. Block two hours, once a week, to batch. In that window, shoot 5 to 7 short clips and photos of your food, your drinks, and your room. Batching beats trying to post live every single day.
  3. Post 3 to 4 times a week, and use Stories daily for specials and behind-the-scenes moments. Stories are quick and forgiving.
  4. Reply to every comment and direct message within a day. A fast reply about hours or a reservation is often the whole reason someone chooses you.
  5. Track one number: covers on your slow night. If it climbs over a few weeks, keep going. If not, change the offer or the content, not just the effort.

If you can hold that routine for 90 days, you will either build real momentum or prove to yourself that you need help. Both outcomes are useful.

sections.h2: How do you choose? Match it to your budget, your time, and your stage
sections.html:
Here is the simple framework. Run your situation through three filters (budget, time, and stage) and the answer usually picks itself.

By budget

  • Under about $800 a month: do it yourself, or bring on a very part-time freelancer for a few posts. An agency at this level would be templated posting, not real marketing.
  • Around $800 to $1,800 a month: a freelance manager or an entry-level agency package. You get a consistent, professional feed for one or two platforms.
  • $1,800 to $3,000 a month and up: a growth-tier agency with monthly in-person shoots and light ads. For most independent Miami restaurants, this is the realistic sweet spot.

By time

  • You have 5 or more hours a week and you enjoy it: doing it yourself is genuinely viable, at least to start.
  • You have a couple of hours to direct someone, but not to create: a freelance manager fits.
  • You have no time at all: an agency, because managing even one freelancer is itself a job.

By stage

  • Brand-new and watching every dollar: do it yourself to find your voice and see what your audience responds to.
  • Established and steady, and you want to look more professional: a freelancer or an entry agency.
  • Growing, adding locations, or leaning on ads: an agency that can scale with you.

If you want it as a quick decision tree, ask yourself these in order:

  1. Do I have 5 or more hours a week and actually enjoy this? If yes, and money is tight, do it yourself and revisit in 90 days.
  2. Do I have a modest budget and someone reliable to manage? Hire a freelance manager on a one-month trial.
  3. Do I need steady content, in-person video, and ads, with no time to manage anyone? Hire an agency.

One Miami note that cuts across all three: this is a dense, highly visual, and heavily bilingual market. Whatever you choose has to post in both English and Spanish, and it should be at full strength during tourist season, roughly December through April, when Brickell, Wynwood, Miami Beach, and Coral Gables fill up and the competition for attention is fiercest.

sections.h2: Red flags to avoid, whichever option you pick
sections.html:
Some warning signs apply to a freelancer and an agency equally. If you spot these during the sales conversation, keep looking.

  • One all-in price with no breakout for ad spend. A clear vendor tells you what is management labor and what actually buys reach on Meta or TikTok. If they blur the two, you do not know what you are paying for.
  • A $99-a-month 'we post for you' plan. At that price there is no in-person shooting. You are buying scheduling software and a few stock or templated posts, not marketing that fills tables.
  • A long contract with no trial period. Good people will let you start with a month. A twelve-month lock with no exit is a bet on their sales pitch, not their work.
  • They cannot show a restaurant feed they built from zero. General 'social media' samples are not the same as growing a real restaurant account. Ask to see one and watch how they answer.
  • Guarantees of followers or 'going viral.' Nobody can promise that honestly. A real partner talks about consistency and reservations, not magic numbers.
  • They never come shoot in person. A feed built only from your phone dumps and stock photos looks like everyone else's. Original, on-site content is the whole point.
  • No bilingual ability, in Miami. If they cannot write and reply in Spanish, they are only reaching half your neighborhood.
  • They are slow to reply to you now. If responses drag during the courtship, they will not get faster once you have signed.

sections.h2: What 'good' looks like once you decide
sections.html:
Whichever path you choose, the marks of a healthy setup are the same. Hold your manager, your agency, or yourself to this short list.

  • Content that looks like your place, shot on-site, not pulled from a stock library. Someone is capturing your actual food and room on a regular basis.
  • Consistent posting, week in and week out, without long silent stretches. A steady rhythm beats occasional bursts.
  • Fast replies to comments, direct messages, and reviews. Every unanswered question about hours or reservations is a table you may have lost.
  • Ads and organic working together, with paid spend clearly separated from the fee and aimed at your actual neighborhood.
  • Plain-English reporting tied to real outcomes, like covers on your slow nights and reservations, not just likes.
  • Bilingual coverage, in both English and Spanish, because that is simply how Miami eats and scrolls.

Set a 90-day checkpoint no matter which option you pick. Are your slow nights fuller? Are you seeing more saves, shares, direct messages, and reservations? If the honest answer is yes, keep going. If it is no, change the plan before you spend more, because effort aimed at the wrong thing is just expensive motion.

If you reach that checkpoint and realize you need a team that shoots, posts, replies, and runs ads for restaurants in this exact market, that is what our restaurant social media marketing service is built to be. And if you decide a freelancer or doing it yourself is the smarter move for you right now, that is a perfectly good answer too.

faqs.q: Is a social media manager or an agency better for a restaurant?
faqs.a: Neither is automatically better. A social media manager (a single freelancer or in-house employee) is cheaper and more personal, but it is one person and you have to manage them. An agency costs more and gives you a team that shoots, posts, replies, and runs ads, and owns the result. Choose a manager if your budget is modest and you like staying involved. Choose an agency if you need steady content, in-person video, and ads, and have no time to supervise a hire.

faqs.q: How much does a restaurant social media manager cost compared to an agency?
faqs.a: A freelance social media manager usually charges $25 to $75 per hour, and often packages restaurant work at $800 to $1,500 a month. A full-time in-house hire in the Miami area runs roughly $50,000 to $70,000 a year in salary, plus taxes and benefits. Agencies typically start around $1,500 a month, with growth programs at $1,800 to $3,000 and full-service work at $2,500 to $5,000 or more. Ad spend is separate from all of these, usually $500 to $1,500 a month.

faqs.q: Can I just do my restaurant's social media myself?
faqs.a: Yes, and many owners should start there. Doing it yourself is free in dollars, gives you full control, and can produce the most authentic content, since nobody knows your food better than you. The catch is time and consistency: done well it takes 5 to 10 hours a week, and it is the first task that gets dropped on a busy night. It works best when you are brand-new, watching every dollar, or genuinely enjoy it. Pick one platform, batch your content weekly, and reassess in 90 days.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a freelance social media manager and an agency?
faqs.a: A freelancer is one independent person who runs your accounts, usually for several clients at once, at a lower cost. An agency is a company with a small team of specialists (a shooter, an editor, a writer, an ad manager) that runs your social media as a service. The freelancer is cheaper and more personal but can leave gaps when they are busy or away, and you remain their manager. The agency costs more but provides coverage that does not rest on one person, and it owns the outcome.

faqs.q: If I hire someone, do I still have to pay for ads separately?
faqs.a: Almost always, yes. Whether you hire a freelancer or an agency, their fee pays for the labor of planning, creating, posting, and reporting. The money that actually buys reach on Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok comes out of your own ad account as a separate line. Budget at least $500 to $1,500 a month for paid reach on top of the management fee, and ask any vendor to spell out exactly how much of what you pay reaches a real ad account.

faqs.q: How do I know if a social media manager or agency is any good?
faqs.a: Ask three questions and insist on a trial. First, how often do you come shoot original content in person at my restaurant? Second, is ad spend included in your fee or billed separately, and how much reaches a real ad account? Third, can you show me a restaurant feed you built from scratch? Then start with a one-month paid trial instead of a long contract, and judge them on whether they posted on time and whether the content actually looks like your place. Walk away from anyone who guarantees followers or hides how ad spend is split.

faqs.q: When should a restaurant stop doing social media itself and hire help?
faqs.a: Make the switch when consistency breaks down or growth stalls. The clearest signals are a feed that keeps going quiet for weeks because the dining room got busy, content that has plateaued, or a point where you want to add paid ads and do not have the expertise. If you have hit a 90-day stretch where you could not keep up, that is your sign to bring on a freelancer or an agency. Many owners start in-house to find their voice, then hand it off once the work outgrows their free hours.

faqs.q: Should a Miami restaurant hire someone who works in Spanish?
faqs.a: Yes. A large share of Miami diners read, search, and scroll in Spanish, so bilingual posting and replies are not a nice extra here, they are table stakes. Whether you choose a freelancer, an agency, or do it yourself, your captions, Stories, and community replies should run in both English and Spanish. If a vendor cannot create and respond in Spanish, they are only reaching half of your neighborhood, and in a market this competitive that is a real disadvantage.
